column2: This one supports himself in two ways: as this breath, and as that sun. These two are the two courses, inner and outer, by day and night; they revolve. That sun is the outer self; the breath is the inner self; the outer self is inferred by the inner one through movement — "movement," so it is said. Whoever, a knower with sins removed, unshaken in vision, pure in mind, devoted to that, with eyes turned inward — he too, the inner self, is inferred from the outer self by movement. Now, this golden Person who is within the sun, who sees me as golden — he abides in the lotus of the heart within and eats food.

Now he who abides in the lotus of the heart and eats food is this fire, situated in heaven, of the sun, called Time, unseen, who eats all beings as food. "What is the lotus? Of what is it made?" This space is that lotus; these four quarters and four intermediate quarters are its petals; the fire below and the sun above are the breath and the sun. Let one worship these with the syllable Om, with the Vyahritis and with the Savitri.

There are two forms of Brahman: the formed and the formless. What is formed is untrue; what is formless is true — that is Brahman, that is light; what is light is the sun. This sun became Om as the Self; he divided himself threefold: Om has three measures, by which all this is woven, warp and woof, in him. So it is said: "This sun is Om." Meditating thus, let him yoke the Self.

It is said elsewhere: that which is the Udgitha is the Pranava, and that which is the Pranava is the Udgitha; that sun is the Udgitha and the Pranava. Thus it is said: the Udgitha, called Pranava, the Leader, form of light, without sleep, ageless, deathless, to be known fivefold, hidden in the cave. Thus it is said: Brahman has its root above and its branches down to Brahma — space, air, fire, water, earth and the rest — eaten by one. That Brahman is its splendour, which is the sun, and this splendour belongs to the syllable Om. Therefore let him worship it constantly with Om — one is awakened to its essence. Thus it is said: this syllable alone is holy; knowing this syllable, whoever wishes for anything obtains it.

It is said elsewhere: this is its body, which is Om — the one with sound, the one with gender (woman, man, neuter), the one with radiance (fire, air, sun), the one with a lord (Rudra, Vishnu), the one with a mouth (the Garhapatya, Dakshina and Ahavaniya fires), the one with knowledge (Rig, Yajus, Saman), the one with worlds (bhuh, bhuvah, svah), the one with time (past, present, future), the one with heat (breath, fire, sun), the one with nourishment (food, water, moon), the one with awareness (intellect, mind, ego), the one with life (prana, apana, vyana). "Some, saying 'I give up,' offer these"; thus it is said. This, O Satyakama, is the higher and the lower Brahman, which is the syllable Om.

This was indeed unmanifest; Prajapati, the True, having practised austerity, uttered "bhuh, bhuvah, svah." This is Prajapati's grossest body, the one with worlds: svah is its head, bhuvah its navel, bhuh its feet, the sun its eye — for a person's great measure depends on the eye, and with the eye one moves among measures; the eye is truth; a person established in the eye speaks in all matters. Therefore let one worship "bhuh, bhuvah, svah"; by this Prajapati, the Self of all, the eye of all, is worshipped. Thus it is said: this is Prajapati's body that bears the universe; in it all this is hidden, and it is hidden in all this. Therefore let one worship it.

That excellent (varenyam) of Savitr — that sun is Savitr; "he is to be chosen by one who desires the Self," say the knowers of Brahman. "We meditate on the splendour (bhargas) of the God" — Savitr is God, and we meditate on what is called his splendour, say the knowers of Brahman. "Who may impel our thoughts" — thoughts are intellects; "who may impel ours," say the knowers of Brahman. Then "bhargas": that which is placed in that sun and in the pupil of the eye is called bhargas; it "shines" (bha), "colours" (ra) these beings, and beings "go" (ga) into it and come from it. Therefore, because of bearing, it is bhargas; because of impelling enemies, it is Surya; because of pressing out, it is Savitr; because of giving, it is Aditya; because of purifying, it is Pavamana; because of moving, it is Aditya. Thus it is said of the Self: the Self, called immortal, is the thinker, knower, goer, creator, gladdener, doer, speaker, taster, smeller, and toucher — the all-pervading one, established in the body. Where there is duality in awareness, there one hears, sees, smells, tastes and touches: the Self knows all. Where awareness has become non-dual, free from cause and effect, indescribable, incomparable, without characteristics — what can be said of that?

This Self is the Lord (Ishana), Shambhu, Bhava, Rudra, Prajapati, the creator of the universe, Hiranyagarbha, Truth, Breath, the Swan, the Tranquil, Vishnu, Narayana, the Sun, Savitr, the Creator, the Sovereign, Indra, the Moon. He who burns, covered with fire, with a thousand-eyed golden bliss — he is to be sought and searched for. Having given fearlessness to all beings and gone to the forest, having cast outward the objects of the senses, one perceives him from one's own body: "the one of universal form, the golden, the all-knowing, the final refuge, the one light, the burning; the thousand-rayed, existing in a hundred ways — the breath of creatures, this sun, rises."

This one supports himself in two ways: as this breath, and as that sun. These are his two paths, inner and outer, by day and night; they revolve. That sun is the outer self; the breath is the inner self; the inner self is therefore inferred from the outer by movement — "movement," so it is said. Whoever, a knower with sins removed, controller of the senses, pure in mind, devoted to it, with eyes turned inward, is inferred by the inner self from the outer self by movement. Now this golden Person within the sun, who sees this earth as golden, abides in the lotus of the heart within and eats food.

Now he who abides in the lotus of the heart and eats food is this fire, situated in heaven, of the sun, called Time, unseen, who eats all beings as food. "What is the lotus, and of what is it made?" This space is that lotus; these four quarters and four intermediate quarters are its petals; the breath and the sun move up to it here. Let one worship these with the syllable Om, with the Vyahritis and with the Savitri.

There are two forms of Brahman: the formed and the formless. What is formed is untrue; what is formless is true — that is Brahman, that is light; what is light is the sun. This became Om as the Self; he divided himself threefold: Om has three measures, by which all this is woven, warp and woof, in him. Thus it is said: this is the sun as Om. Meditating thus, let him yoke the Self.

It is said elsewhere: that which is the Udgitha is the Pranava, and that which is the Pranava is the Udgitha; the sun is the Udgitha and the Pranava. Thus it is said: the Udgitha called Pranava, the Leader, radiant form, without sleep, ageless, deathless, three-footed, three-syllabled, to be known again fivefold, hidden in the cave. Thus it is said: Brahman with three feet has its root above; its branches are space, air, fire, water, earth and the rest; it is the one named Ashvattha. This Brahman has this splendour, which is that sun, and the splendour of the syllable Om. Therefore let one worship it constantly with Om — one awakens to it. Thus it is said: this syllable alone is holy, this syllable alone is supreme; knowing this syllable, whoever wishes for anything obtains it.

It is said elsewhere: this is its body, which is Om — the one with sound; the one with gender (woman, man, neuter); the one with radiance (fire, air, sun); the one with a lord (Brahma, Rudra, Vishnu); the one with a mouth (the Garhapatya, Dakshina and Ahavaniya fires); the one with knowledge (Rig, Yajus, Saman); the one with worlds (bhuh, bhuvah, svah); the one with time (past, present, future); the one with heat (breath, fire, sun); the one with nourishment (food, water, moon); the one with awareness (intellect, mind, ego); the one with life (prana, apana, vyana). "By the word Om, these are offered and honoured"; thus it is said. This, O Satyakama, is the higher and the lower Brahman, which is the syllable Om.

This was indeed unuttered; Prajapati, the True, having practised austerity, uttered "bhuh, bhuvah, svah." This is Prajapati's grossest body, the one with worlds: svah is its head, bhuvah its navel, bhuh its feet, the sun its eye — for a person's great measure is spread out by the eye, and with the eye he moves among measures; the eye is truth; a person stationed in the eye moves among all objects. Therefore let one worship "bhuh, bhuvah, svah"; by this Prajapati, the Self of all, the eye of all, is worshipped. Thus it is said: this is Prajapati's body that bears the universe; in it all this is hidden, and it is hidden in all this. Therefore let one worship it.

That excellent of Savitr — that sun is Savitr; he is to be chosen by one who desires the Self, say the knowers of Brahman. "We meditate on the splendour of the God" — Savitr is God, and we meditate on what is called his splendour, say the knowers of Brahman. "Who may impel our thoughts" — thoughts are intellects; may he impel ours, say the knowers of Brahman. Then "bhargas": that which is placed in that sun and in the pupil of the eye is called bhargas; it burns up (bharjayati) — this is bhargas, says Rudra, among knowers of Brahman. Then "bha": it makes these worlds shine; "ra": it colours these beings; "ga": beings go into it and come from it. Therefore, from bearing, it is bhargas; from impelling enemies, Surya; from pressing out, Savitr; from taking, Aditya; from purifying, Pavana; and from moving, Aditya. Thus it is said of the Self: the leader, called immortal, the thinker, the goer, the emitter, gladdener, doer, speaker, taster, smeller, seer, hearer, toucher — the all-pervading one established in the body. Where there is duality in awareness, there one hears, sees, smells, tastes and touches: the Self knows all. Where awareness has become non-dual, free of cause, effect and action, indescribable, incomparable, without characteristics — what is that? It cannot be spoken.

This Self is the Lord, Shambhu, Bhava, Rudra, Prajapati, the creator of the universe, Hiranyagarbha, Truth, Breath, the Swan, the Ruler, Vishnu, Narayana, the Sun, Savitr, the Creator, the Establisher, the Sovereign, Indra, the Moon. He who burns like fire, covered by fire, by a thousand-eyed golden egg — he is to be sought and searched for. Having given fearlessness to all beings and gone to the forest, having turned the objects of the senses outward, one perceives him from one's own body. "The one of universal form, the golden, the all-knowing, the final refuge, the one light, the burning; the thousand-rayed, existing in a hundred ways — the breath of creatures, this sun, rises."

Therefore, knowing himself to be of both natures, he meditates on the Self in the Self alone, and sacrifices in the Self alone; meditation is established in practice, the mind is praised by the wise. "The mind is impure, struck by leavings" — with this he should purify it. He recites the mantra: "What is left over, what is contaminated by leavings, what has been given by a sinful person, or comes from a death- or birth-impurity — let fire, the rays of Savitr, and the treasure purify that food of mine and whatever other wrong I have done." With water he first surrounds the food; he offers five oblations: "To prana, svaha; to apana, svaha; to vyana, svaha; to samana, svaha; to udana, svaha." Then, eating what remains in silence, he again surrounds it above with water; having sipped water, he meditates on the Self with two verses: "You are the breath, the fire," and "You are the All." "Breath and fire, the Supreme Self, resting on the five winds — may he, pleased, please the universe, the enjoyer of the universe. You are the universe; you are Vaishvanara; the universe, when it is born, is held by you; and all the oblations enter you; the creatures are there where you are the immortal." He who does so, by this rite, does not again attain the state of being eaten.

Now there is something further to be known: a later modification of this sacrifice of the Self — what the food is and who the eater. Its explanation: the Person is the conscious one, abiding within Pradhana (Nature); he alone is the enjoyer and enjoys the food of Nature. His elemental self is the food; the doer is Nature. Therefore what is enjoyed is threefold in quality, and the enjoyer is the Person within. Here what is seen is called the perception; since animals arise from seed, seed is what is enjoyed; by this the enjoyability of Pradhana is explained. Therefore the Person is the enjoyer, Nature is enjoyed, and the one abiding in it enjoys — the food is of Nature, transformed into the divisions of the three qualities, from the Great Principle down to the particular ones; by this the account of the fourteenfold path is given. This world, made of pleasure, pain and delusion, is food; for a seed has no relish of its own until it sprouts. It too has the nature of food in three stages — childhood, youth and old age — through transformation. So Nature's being food is perceived in its manifest state; there the intellect and the like become the tasty things — determination, intention and self-conceit; then the five objects of sense become tasty; likewise all the actions of the senses and of the breaths. Thus food is manifest and unmanifest. Its enjoyer is without qualities, and his being an enjoyer is well known as consciousness. As fire is the eater of the gods' food and Soma is the food, so — thus the knower: the elemental self is called Soma, and fire too has an unmanifest mouth; by this statement the Person enjoys the threefold through an unmanifest mouth. He who knows this is a renunciant, a yogi, and one who sacrifices in the Self. And just as none touches the sense-objects of women who have entered an empty house, so he who does not touch the objects that have entered is a renunciant, a yogi, and one who sacrifices in the Self.

This is the supreme form of the Self: food; for this breath is made of food. If one does not eat, one becomes unable to think, hear, touch, see, speak, smell or taste, and gives up the breaths — thus it is said. But if one eats, being rich in breath one becomes able to think, hear, touch, speak, taste, smell and see — thus it is said. From food, creatures are born, whatever dwell on the earth; then by food they live; and at the end they too go into it.

It is said elsewhere: all these beings fall daily, seeking to seize food; the sun takes up food with his rays, and by it he burns; sprinkled with food, these breaths cook; fire blazes with food; this was arranged by Brahman for one desiring food. Therefore let one worship food as the Self. Thus it is said: from food beings are born; being born, they grow by food; beings are eaten and they eat; therefore it is called food.

It is said elsewhere: this is the body of the venerable Vishnu called "Bearer of the universe" — this food. Breath is the essence of food; mind of breath; knowledge of mind; bliss of knowledge. He who knows this becomes one with food, with breath, with mind, with knowledge, with bliss. As many beings as eat food here, he who knows this eats food within them. Food alone is the remedy for old age; food is called the gatherer; food is the breath of animals; food is the eldest; food is called the physician.

It is said elsewhere: food is the source of all this, and Time is the source of food; the sun is the source of Time. Its form is that which is gathered from moments and the like — the year of twelve parts. Half of this is of Agni, half of Varuna, beginning with Magha and ending with the half of Shravishtha for Agni; in reverse order, from Sarpa to the end of Shravishtha for Soma. In it, each of the nine parts belongs to the self, along with the course of the planets. Because of subtlety this is the measure, and by it time is measured; without a measure there is no knowledge of the measured, and the measured too becomes a measure by being separate — for the sake of self-knowledge. Thus it is said: in as many divisions of time as there are, that one moves; he who worships Time as Brahman — time recedes very far from him. Thus it is said: from time beings flow forth; from time they grow; in time they come to rest; time has form and is formless.

There are two forms of Brahman: Time and the timeless. What is before the sun is timeless; what begins with the sun is Time, with parts. The form of what has parts is the year. From the year these creatures are born; by the year, once born, they grow; in the year they go to rest. Therefore the year is Prajapati, Time, food, the nest of Brahman, and the Self. Thus it is said: Time cooks all beings in the great Self; he who knows in whom Time is cooked — he is the knower of the Veda.

This Time has a body; it is the king of the oceans of creatures. Abiding in this is the one named Savitr, from whom the moon, the stars, the planets, the years and the like are begotten; and from them all this, whatever good or bad is seen in this world, comes. Therefore Brahman is the Self of the sun; let one worship the sun called Time. "The sun is Brahman," say some; thus it is said: the sacrificer, the enjoyer, the oblation, the mantra, the sacrifice, Vishnu, Prajapati — the All, the lord, the witness who shines in yonder orb.

Brahman was indeed this in the beginning: One, infinite to the east, infinite to the south, infinite to the west, infinite to the north, infinite above and below — infinite on all sides. For the directions east and the rest do not apply to it, nor do the across and the above. This Supreme Self is immeasurable, beyond reason, inconceivable; he is the Self of space; he alone, at the end of all, remains awake. From this space he awakens all this to mere consciousness; by him alone this is meditated on, and in him it comes to rest. His radiant form is that which burns in yonder sun, and the light in the smokeless fire, and the wonderfully varied fire in the belly which cooks food. Thus it is said: he who is in the fire, he who is in the heart here, and he who is in the sun — he is one. He who knows this attains oneness with the One.

It is said elsewhere: when the knower, having restrained the mind from outside and set the breath in the sense-objects, remains free of intention — since from the breathless the living being, called breath, arises here, therefore let him hold the breath in the "fourth" (turiya). Thus it is said: the mindless is placed in the middle of the mind, inconceivable, secret, supreme; let one fix the mind there, and that support-free sign.

It is said elsewhere: beyond this is the concentration: by pressing the palate with the tip of the tongue, by restraining speech, mind and breath, one sees Brahman through reasoning. When by the Self one sees the Self, smaller than the small, shining, through the destruction of the mind, then, having seen the Self by the Self, one becomes selfless; being selfless, one is unlimited, sourceless, inconceivable — this is the mark of liberation, the supreme secret. Thus it is said: by the serenity of the mind one destroys good and bad action; with a serene self, abiding in the Self, one enjoys imperishable happiness.

It is said elsewhere: the upward channel called Sushumna, along which the breath moves, is divided within the palate; by it, joined with breath, Om and mind, let him go upward. Turning the tip of the tongue toward the palate and not joining the senses, let him behold greatness by greatness. Then he attains selflessness; through selflessness he does not experience pleasure or pain; he attains isolation. Thus it is said: "Having first established the Supreme, and then having restrained the breath, having crossed to the shore by the shoreless, let him afterward unite at the crown of the head."

It is said elsewhere: there are two Brahmans to be meditated on: sound and soundless. By sound alone the soundless is revealed. There, Om is the sound; by it he rises upward and comes to rest in the soundless. This is the way, this is the immortal, this is union with it, this is peace — and so it is. Then, as a spider climbs upward by its thread and gains open space, so this meditator, rising by Om, gains independence. Others, who speak of sound, hear the sound of the space in the heart by joining the ear and the thumb; its likeness is sevenfold: like rivers, a bell, a brass vessel, a wheel, the croak of a frog, rain, and speech in a windless place. Having passed beyond these distinct characteristics, they go to rest in the soundless, unmanifest Brahman, and there they become undivided, undiscriminated, like various juices that have become one honey. Thus it is said: two Brahmans are to be known — sound-Brahman and the Supreme; he who is versed in the sound-Brahman reaches the Supreme Brahman.

It is said elsewhere: the sound that is the syllable Om — its tip is tranquil, soundless, fearless, sorrowless, blissful, satisfied, steady, unmoving, immortal, unfallen, firm, called Vishnu; therefore let one worship that for the sake of the highest. Thus it is said: "That which is the highest and the lower, the god, named Om — soundless and empty, let him practise it at the crown of the head."

It is said elsewhere: the bow is the body, Om is the arrow, and its tip is the mind. Piercing the darkness that is its mark, one comes to what is not covered by darkness. Then, having pierced that which is covered, one sees, beyond darkness, Brahman flashing like a whirling firebrand, of the colour of the sun, full of energy — that which shines in yonder sun, in the moon, in fire, in lightning. Having seen it, one attains immortality. Thus it is said: meditation is established in the supreme inner principle and in the objects of concentration; therefore undifferentiated knowledge attains differentiation. And when the mind has dissolved, the bliss that is witnessed by the Self — that is Brahman, the immortal, the pure; that is the goal; that is the world.

It is said elsewhere: as if in sleep, with the senses withdrawn, by an intellect most pure, one sees as in a dream — unhindered in the aperture of the senses — the one called Pranava, the Leader, form of light, sleepless, ageless, deathless, sorrowless; he too becomes Pranava, the Leader, of the form of light, sleepless, ageless, deathless and sorrowless. Thus it is said: "Thus breath and Om, since he yokes everything in many ways, or since all is yoked, is remembered as Yoga. The oneness of breath, mind and senses, and the giving up of all states of being, is called Yoga."

It is said elsewhere: as a fowler draws up water-creatures with a thread-machine and offers them in the fire in his belly, so he draws up these breaths with Om and offers them in the healthy fire. From this, as a hot ghee is kindled by touch with straw and wood, so the one called breathless is kindled by touching the breath. And what is kindled is Brahman's form, the supreme abode of Vishnu, and Rudra's Rudrahood; dividing itself in immeasurable ways, it fills these worlds. Thus it is said: "As sparks from a fire and rays from the sun, so from him breath and the rest again rise up here in due order."

It is said elsewhere: this is the light of the Supreme Brahman, immortal and bodiless; the warmth of the body is its ghee; being manifest, it is placed in space. They stir the space of the heart with one-pointed mind, and it becomes as light. From that, one soon attains that state — as an iron ball placed on earth soon becomes earth, and as an iron ball set in soft clay, though smiths and others work it, is not overcome, so the mind is destroyed along with its support. Thus it is said: "The sheath made of the space of the heart, bliss, the supreme abode — that is our own yoga; and the light of fire and of the sun."

It is said elsewhere: having passed beyond the elements and the objects of the senses, then, having renounced, taking the bow of firmness as a staff and the arrow of freedom from conceit, he strikes down the guardian at the door of Brahman. The chief is delusion as his helmet, craving and envy as his earrings, drowsiness and sloth as his quiver, self-conceit as the commander, anger as the bowstring, the staff of greed as his bow, and with the arrow of desire he kills these beings. Having killed him, he crosses to the far side of the space of the heart by the boat of Om; when the inner space is revealed, slowly, like one seeking ore, he enters, and so enters the hall of Brahman; then, with the teacher's instruction, he should drive out the four-fold sheath of Brahman. Then, pure, cleansed, empty, tranquil, breathless, selfless, infinite, imperishable, steady, eternal, unborn, independent, he abides in his own greatness. Seeing him abide in his own greatness, he looks upon the wheel of transmigration as upon a rolling wheel. Thus it is said: "For one who is joined for six months and ever free, endless, supreme, secret, right Yoga proceeds. But it does not, ever, for one pierced by rajas and tamas, well inflamed, and attached to sons, wife and family."

Having said this, Shakayanya, who was inward in heart, bowed to him: "By this knowledge of Brahman, O king, the sons of Prajapati have set out on the path of Brahman." He attains contentment, endurance of the opposites, and tranquillity through the practice of yoga. This most secret teaching should not be told to one who is not a son, not a disciple, or not tranquil; let one give it to one of exclusive devotion, endowed with all qualities.

Om. In a pure place, pure, established in goodness, studying the true, speaking the true, meditating on the true, sacrificing to the true — let him be so. Therefore, established in the true Brahman, longing for the true, freed from the fruits of action, with bonds cut, without expectation, fearless toward others as toward himself, free from desire, he stands, having reached imperishable, immeasurable happiness. Freedom from desire is the supreme rescue, as if from a treasure-house of the Supreme. The Person full of all desires, marked by determination, intention and self-conceit, is bound; therefore the opposite is liberated. Here some say: bound by the difference in the qualities of Nature, the self falls into bondage through determination; from the destruction of the faults of determination there is liberation. By the mind alone one sees, by the mind alone one hears; desire, intention, doubt, faith, faithlessness, steadiness, unsteadiness, shame, wisdom and fear — all this is the mind. Carried along by floods of qualities, defiled, unsteady, fickle, greedy, longing and distracted, it falls into conceit, thinking, "I am he; this is mine," and binds the self by the self, like a bird in a net. Therefore the Person, marked by determination, intention and self-conceit, is bound; the opposite is liberated. Therefore let one remain without determination, without intention, without self-conceit — this is the mark of liberation. This is here the way to Brahman; this is here the door-opening; by this one goes beyond this darkness. Here all desires are gathered. On this they quote: "When the five kinds of knowledge stand still together with the mind, and the intellect does not stir — that they call the highest state." Having said this, Shakayanya, inward in heart, bowed to him; the king, having duly served him, his task done, went north; for there is no going by a devious path here. This is the way of Brahman here; having pierced the door of the sun, they go out upward — on this they quote: "Endless are his rays, standing like a lamp in the heart — white and black, tawny and blue, brown, and softly red. Of them one stands upward; whoever, piercing the orb of the sun and passing beyond the world of Brahma, goes by it, goes to the highest state. The other hundred rays stand upward; by them one enters the abodes of the hosts of gods. Those rays of soft light that are of many forms and below — by them, here, for the enjoyment of action, the helpless one wanders." Therefore that venerable sun is the cause of creation, heaven and release.

Of what nature are these senses that move about, and who is their controller here? — so he asks. He answers: "They are of the nature of the Self; for the Self is their controller. The Apsarases, the sunlight-rays called Marichis, with five rays eat objects." "Which is the Self?" "He who is called pure, cleansed, empty, tranquil and the like, and who is to be grasped by his own marks. His mark, though he has no mark, is the heat pervading fire, and in water the most auspicious essence" — so some say. Others say: speech, ear, eye, mind, breath; others: intellect, firmness, memory, wisdom. These are of him as sprouts are of a seed, or as smoke, flame and sparks are of fire. On this they quote: "As sparks from a fire and rays from the sun, so from him breath and the rest again rise up here in due order."

From this Self, therefore, all breaths, all worlds, all Vedas, all gods and all beings arise — its Upanishad is "the Truth of truth." As from a fire kindled with wet fuel separate clouds of smoke go forth, so this is the breath of this great Being: the Rig Veda, Yajur Veda, Sama Veda, Atharvangirasa, history, ancient lore, sciences, Upanishads, verses, sutras, explanations and commentaries — all these beings are its.

This fire with five bricks is the year. Its bricks are spring, summer, the rains, autumn and winter; it has a head, two wings, a back and a tail. This is the fire known to the Person: it is Prajapati's first piling. With its rays, having thrown the sacrificer up into the sky, it gave him to the wind. The wind is breath; breath is fire; its bricks are prana, vyana, apana, samana and udana; it has a head, two wings, a back and a tail. This is the fire known to the Person; this atmosphere is Prajapati's second piling. With its rays, having thrown the sacrificer up into heaven, it gave him to Indra. That sun is Indra; this is fire; its bricks are the Rig, Yajus, Saman, Atharvangirasa, history and ancient lore; it has a head, two wings, a back and a tail. This is the fire known to the Person; this heaven is Prajapati's third piling. With its rays, the knower of the Self makes an offering of the sacrificer — he sends him up to Brahman; there he becomes joyful and delighted.

The earth is the Garhapatya fire, the atmosphere is the Dakshina fire, heaven is the Ahavaniya fire; from these alone the purifying (Pavamana, Pavaka and Shuchi) fires are revealed by this sacrifice — for the gastric fire is a union of Pavamana, Pavaka and Shuchi. Therefore the fire is to be worshipped, piled, praised and meditated on; the sacrificer, having taken the oblation, wishes to meditate on the deity: "The golden-coloured bird is established in the heart and in the sun; the diver, the swan, the bull of light — we sacrifice to him in this fire." He also examines the meaning of the mantra: "That excellent splendour of Savitr" is to be meditated on; he who, established in the intellect, meditates here, follows the path of peace of mind and places it in the Self alone. On this there are these verses: (1) As a fire without fuel becomes quiet in its own source, so the mind, with its activities ceased, becomes quiet in its own source. (2) For the mind that has become quiet in its own source, having true desire, deluded by sense-objects, the falsehoods that follow from action come to nothing. (3) The mind alone is the cycle of birth and death; let one purify it with effort; what one's mind is, that one becomes — this is the eternal secret. (4) By the serenity of the mind one destroys good and bad action; with a serene self, abiding in the Self, one enjoys imperishable happiness. (5) As the mind of a creature is attached to the field of sense-objects, if it were so attached to Brahman, who would not be freed from bondage? (6) The mind is said to be of two kinds, pure and impure: impure through contact with desire, pure when free from desire. (7) Having made the mind free of dullness and distraction, perfectly still, when it reaches the state of no-mind, that is the highest state. (8) The mind should be restrained in the heart until it has come to its end; this is knowledge and this is liberation; the rest is an expansion of books. (9) The happiness that the mind, whose impurity has been washed away by absorption and which is settled in the Self, obtains, cannot be described in words; it is then grasped by the inner organ itself. (10) As water in water, fire in fire, space in space is not distinguished, so he whose mind has gone within is set free. (11) The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation of human beings: attached to sense-objects, bondage; free of objects, liberation. Therefore for those who do not keep the sacred fires, do not pile the fire, and do not know it, the Brahmin's remembering the pathway of space is contrary; hence the fire is to be worshipped, piled, praised and meditated on.

Homage to Agni, dweller on earth, remembered in the world: give this sacrificer a world. Homage to Vayu, dweller in the atmosphere, remembered in the world: give this sacrificer a world. Homage to the Sun, dweller in heaven, remembered in the world: give this sacrificer a world. Homage to Brahman, dweller in all, remembered in all: give this sacrificer all. With a golden vessel the face of truth is covered; uncover it, O Pushan, for one whose duty is truth — to Vishnu. He who is the Person in yonder sun, I am he. This is the true law: that the sun's being the sun is that white Person, without mark, a mere portion of the light within space — what is in the middle of the sun, as it were, and in the eye and in the fire: this is Brahman, this is the immortal, this is bhargas, this is the law of truth. It is a mere portion of the light within space; what is in the middle of the sun shines as the Yajus, the Om, the waters, the light, the essence, the immortal, Brahman — bhuh, bhuvah, svah, Om. "The eight-footed, pure Swan, the three-stranded, minute, imperishable — the dual-natured, blind by light, kindled by light, seeing all, he sees." A mere portion of the light within space, what is in the middle of the sun, at rising with rays, becomes: this is Savitr, this is the law of truth, this is the Yajus, this is austerity, this is fire, this is wind, this is breath, this is water, this is the moon, this is the bright, this is the immortal, this is the domain of Brahman, this is the ray, the ocean; in it the sacrificer dissolves like salt in water. This indeed is oneness with Brahman; here all desires are gathered. On this they quote: "Like a stream of fine dust carried by the wind, the one who is within the gods flashes; he who knows this becomes a knower, a knower of duality, and enters into the one abode and becomes of that nature. Those who, like sparks, rise up ceaselessly — like lightning from a cloud's flame — in the highest heaven, they are the rays, dwelling in glory; like matted locks, they are those whose path is the dark."

There are indeed these two forms of the light of Brahman: one tranquil and one flourishing. What is tranquil has space as its support; what is flourishing has this as its food. Therefore one should sacrifice with mantras, herbs, ghee, meat, cakes and cooked offerings, inside the altar, and with the remaining foods and drinks, regarding one's own mouth as the Ahavaniya fire — for the increase of radiance, for the conquest of holy worlds and for immortality. On this they quote: "Let one who desires heaven offer the Agnihotra; by the Agnishtoma he wins the realm of Yama; by the Ukthya the realm of Soma; by the Shodashin the realm of the Sun; by the Atiratra self-rule; by the sacrifice lasting a thousand years, the realm of Prajapati." "As a lamp stands by the union of wick, support and oil, so the two, the self and its light, stand by the union with the inner egg."

Therefore let one worship it with Om: the immeasurable radiance, spoken of as threefold — in fire, in the sun, in breath. Then this channel is rich in food; what is offered in fire reaches the sun; from it the essence that flowed forth rains as the Udgitha; by it these breaths, and from the breaths creatures. On this they quote: "What oblation is offered in the fire reaches the sun; the sun rains it by his rays; from it comes food; from food the arising of beings." Thus it is said: "The offering properly made in the fire approaches the sun; from the sun comes rain; from rain, food; then creatures."

He who offers the Agnihotra tears the net of greed. Having cut through delusion, without praising anger, meditating on desire, having then broken through the four-fold sheath of Brahman, he goes to the supreme space: for here, having pierced the circles of the solar, lunar, fiery and sattvic, he then, purified, sees the one who stands within sattva — the unmoving, immortal, unfallen, firm, called Vishnu, the supreme abode of all, endowed with true desire and omniscience, independent, consciousness, abiding in his own greatness. On this they quote: "In the middle of the sun stands the Moon; in the middle of the Moon, the fire; in the middle of light stands goodness; in the middle of goodness stands the Unfallen." Meditating on him who is of the measure of a thumb in the body, and yet smaller than the atom in his connection, he goes to the highest state. Here all desires are gathered; on this they quote: "Of the measure of a thumb, of the extent of the body, like the strength of a lamp, he is threefold; that Brahman, being praised, the great God, entered the worlds." Om. Homage to Brahman, homage.

Fire, the Gayatri, the Trivrit, the Rathantara, spring, breath, the stars, the Vasus — these rise in the east; they burn, rain, praise, re-enter, and look through the interior opening. The inconceivable, the formless, the deep, the enjoyer of qualities, the fearless, the changeless, the Lord of yogis, the all-knowing, the generous, the immeasurable, the beginningless and endless, the glorious, the unborn, the wise, the indescribable, the maker of all, the Self of all, the enjoyer of all, the ruler of all, the inmost of all —

Indra, the Trishtubh, the Panchadasha, the Brihat, summer, vyana, Soma, the Rudras — these rise in the south; they burn, rain, praise, re-enter, and look through the interior opening: the beginningless and endless, the immeasurable, the unbounded, the one who cannot be made to serve another, the independent, the markless, the formless, of endless power, the Creator, the Sun.

The Maruts, the Jagati, the Saptadasha, the Vairupa, the rains, apana, Shukra, the Adityas — these rise in the west; they burn, rain, praise, re-enter, and look through the interior opening: that tranquil, soundless, fearless, sorrowless, blissful, satisfied, steady, unmoving, immortal, unfallen, firm, called Vishnu, the supreme abode of all.

The Vishvedevas, the Anushtubh, the Ekavimsha, the Vairaja, autumn, samana, Varuna, the Sadhyas — these rise in the north; they burn, rain, praise, re-enter, and look through the interior opening: the inwardly pure, cleansed, empty, tranquil, breathless, selfless, infinite.

Mitra and Varuna, the Pankti, the Trinava and Trayastrimsha, the Shakvara and Raivata, the cold seasons, udana, the Angirasas, the Moon — these rise upward; they burn, rain, praise, re-enter, and look through the interior opening: the one called Pranava, the Leader, the form of light, sleepless, ageless, deathless, sorrowless.

Saturn, Rahu, Ketu, snakes, demons, yakshas, men, birds, sharabhas, elephants and the like rise below; they burn, rain, praise, re-enter, and look through the interior opening: he who is the wise one, the supporter, the inmost of all, the imperishable, pure, cleansed, radiant, patient, tranquil.

This Self in the heart within is indeed smaller than the small, like a kindled fire, of universal form; all this is his food; in him these creatures are woven. This Self is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from doubt, free from bonds, whose will is true and whose desire is true. He is the Supreme Lord; he is the lord of beings; he is the protector of beings; he is the bridge, the supporter. This Self is the Lord, Shambhu, Bhava, Rudra, Prajapati, the creator of the universe, Hiranyagarbha, Truth, Breath, the Swan, the Ruler, the Unfallen, Vishnu, Narayana. He who is in the fire, he who is in the heart here, and he who is in the sun — he is one. Homage to him, of universal form, who abides in the true space.

Now, O king, the obstacles to knowledge, this indeed is the source of the net of delusion: those who cling to the "heaven-less" together with heaven, and those others who are always merry, always travelling, always begging, always living by a craft; and those others who beg from villages, who beg from those unfit to sacrifice, disciples of low-born teachers, low-born men who are learned in the scriptures; and those others who are rogues, wanderers, actors, soldiers, mendicants, stage performers, those fallen from royal service, and the like; and those others who, putting forward the interests of yakshas, rakshasas, ghosts, hosts of spirits, ghouls, serpents, planets and the like, say, "We shall pacify them"; and those others who vainly wear ochre robes and earrings, skull-bearers; and those others who through vain arguments, illustrations, tricks and magic wish to take a position on Vedic matters — one should not live with them. They are exposed robbers, unfit for heaven; thus it is said: "Wandering, the world, misled by deceivers who preach selflessness and by false illustrations and reasons, does not know what lies within the knowledge of the Veda."

Brihaspati, having become Shukra, created this ignorance for the safety of Indra and the destruction of the demons. By it they point to the auspicious as inauspicious and the inauspicious as auspicious; they say, "Let there be meditation on a doctrine that harms the Veda and other scriptures." Therefore it should not be studied; otherwise it is barren; its only fruit is pleasure; like one fallen from good conduct, it should not be undertaken. Thus it is said: "Far apart and opposed, going in different directions are what is known as ignorance and what is known as knowledge. I think Nachiketas to be one who desires knowledge; many desires did not tempt you." "He who knows knowledge and ignorance together crosses death by ignorance and attains immortality by knowledge." "Living in the midst of ignorance, thinking themselves wise and learned, the deluded go about, staggering, like blind men led by one who is himself blind."

The gods and the demons, who desired the Self, went to Brahma, bowed to him and said: "Venerable one, we desire the Self; tell us that." After long meditation, he thought that those demons were of a different mind, so he spoke another teaching to them; the deluded ones live by it — attached, injuring the true, speaking falsely, seeing untruth as truth, as in a magic show. Therefore what is set forth in the Vedas is true; those who are learned live by what is said in the Vedas. Therefore a Brahmin should not study what is non-Vedic; let this be the purpose.

This is the form of what is within space, in the sky: the supreme light, spoken of as threefold — in fire, in the sun, in breath. This is the form of what is within space: the syllable Om; by it that awakens, rises and breathes, ceaselessly, resting on the meditation on Brahman — as if in the moving wind, in space, rising by a branch, it moves from trunk to trunk; like a pinch of salt cast into water, like the heat of ghee, like the spreading of the meditator. On this they quote: "Then why is it called electric? Because the moment it is uttered, it illumines the entire body; therefore let him worship the immeasurable light with Om." (1) "The Person who dwells in the right eye is Indra; this Indrani, his wife, dwells in the left eye. (2) Their union is in the cavity within the heart; the red lump of light there is the food of both. (3) From the heart it goes up to the eye and is established in it; that channel is their path — one made two. (4) The mind strikes the fire of the body; it stirs the wind; the wind, moving in the chest, produces a deep sound. (5) In the heart, joined with the fire of space, it is an atom of atoms; in the throat, a double atom; at the tip of the tongue, know a triple atom; issuing forth, it is called the mother-letters. (6) Seeing, he does not see death, nor sickness, nor sorrow; seeing all, he obtains all in every way. (7) The waking one, the dreamer, the deep sleeper, and the one beyond deep sleep — these are the four divisions of him; the fourth is greater than these. (8) In three, Brahman moves with one foot; in the last it moves with three feet; the enjoyment of truth and untruth is the duality of the great soul — the duality of the great soul."
